steps: التصميم المتجاوب يعني تخلي صفحات الويب تظهر بشكل جميل ومناسب على كل الأجهزة، سواء كانت شاشات كمبيوتر ضخمة، أو تابلت، أو موبايل صغير، من غير ما الموقع يتلخبط أو يحصل فيه مشاكل في القراءة.
عشان نعمل كده، بنستخدم استعلامات الوسائط أو اللي بنسميها (Media Queries)، ودي عبارة عن شرط بيكتبه المطور في الكود عشان يفحص حجم شاشة الجهاز، زي مثلاً معرفة عرض الشاشة الحالي.
القاعدة بتتكتب كده: `@media (max-width: 600px)`، ودي معناها إن الـ CSS اللي جوه القوسين دول هيتطبق بس لو عرض الشاشة أصغر من أو بيساوي 600 بكسل، يعني كأننا شغالين على موبايل.
مثال بسيط: ممكن نخلي لون خلفية الموقع أزرق على الشاشات الكبيرة، لكن أول ما العرض يصغر ويدخل جوه نطاق الميديا كويري، الخلفية تتغير للون أخضر عشان تريح عين المستخدم.
القاعدة الذهبية: صمم دائماً الشاشات الصغيرة الأول (Mobile-First)، أو حط الشروط بدقة عشان الموقع يتمدد وينكمش بسلاسة من غير ما المحتوى يهرب بره حدود الشاشة.
الاستخدام في الواقع: المواقع الكبيرة زي اليوتيوب أو متجر إلكتروني بتستعمل الميديا كويري عشان تحول شكل المنتجات من كذا عمود جنب بعض في اللاب توب، لعمود واحد تحت بعض في الموبايل.
ar.example: تخيل إنك بتصمم بطاقة منتج. في الكمبيوتر العرض واسع، فممكن نخلي العنوان والصورة جنب بعض في سطر واحد. لكن لما نفتح الموقع من الموبايل، الشاشة بتكون ضيقة. بنكتب ميديا كويري تقول: لو العرض أقل من 600 بكسل، خلي عرض البطاقة 100% وخلي العناصر تيجي تحت بعضها بدل ما هي جنب بعض. الكود بيبدأ بـ `.card { display: flex; }` وللموبايل `@media (max-width: 600px) { .card { display: block; } }` وده بيخلي البطاقة تتظبط فوراً.
ar.mistake: من الأخطاء المشهورة جداً إننا ننسى نضيف وسم الـ viewport في الـ HTML (`<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">`). من غير الوسسم ده، الموبايل هيتعامل مع الصفحة كأنها شاشة كمبيوتر ضخمة ويصغرها كلها بدل ما يستجيب للميديا كويري. الحل هو دايماً كتابة السطر ده جوه قسم الـ `<head>`.
ar.recap: التصميم المتجاوب واستعلامات الوسائط بيخلوا صفحات الويب تتأقلم مع كل الأجهزة وتغير شكلها تلقائياً. بنستخدم `@media` عشان نغير التخطيطات من متعددة الأعمدة لعمود واحد حسب حجم الشاشة.

q.why: max-width تعني الحد الأقصى للعرض، أي الشاشات الأصغر من أو المساوية لهذا الرقم.

steps: Responsive design means making web pages look gorgeous and work smoothly on all devices, whether it is a giant computer monitor, a tablet, or a tiny smartphone, without breaking or causing reading issues.
To achieve this, developers use Media Queries, which are conditional rules written in CSS to check device screen features, most commonly the current screen width.
A basic rule looks like this: `@media (max-width: 600px)`, meaning the CSS inside these curly braces will only apply if the screen width is smaller than or equal to 600 pixels, like on a phone.
Simple example: We can make the website background blue on large screens, but as soon as the width shrinks into the media query range, the background switches to green to give eyes a break.
The Golden Rule: Always design for small screens first (Mobile-First), or carefully set breakpoints so content stretches and shrinks smoothly without overflowing the screen boundaries.
Real-world use: Major sites like YouTube or online stores use media queries to shift product layouts from multiple horizontal columns on laptops to a single vertical column on mobile phones.
en.example: Imagine designing a product card. On desktop, the screen is wide, so title and image sit side-by-side. On mobile, the screen is narrow. We write a media query stating: if width is below 600px, make card width 100% and stack items vertically. The code starts with `.card { display: flex; }` and for mobile `@media (max-width: 600px) { .card { display: block; } }`, making the card adjust instantly.
en.mistake: A very common beginner mistake is forgetting to add the viewport meta tag in the HTML (`<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">`). Without this tag, mobile browsers pretend they are on a massive desktop screen and scale everything down, ignoring media queries. Fix this by always including that line in `<head>`.
en.recap: Responsive design and media queries let web pages adapt to any device and change layout automatically. We use `@media` to switch layouts from multi-column to single-column based on screen size.

q.why: Media queries help apply different CSS rules depending on the user's screen width.

o: Apply styles when screen width is 768 pixels or less
Apply styles when screen width is greater than 768 pixels

q.t: How do we switch a multi-column desktop layout into a single column on mobile?
o: By deleting all website images entirely
Using a media query that changes layout properties like element width to 100%
By changing the programming language of the page
q.why: We use media queries to adapt layout properties so elements stack nicely in one column.

sections.text: Responsive design is like water taking the shape of its container. Responsive websites shape and adapt to the user's screen size, whether holding a smartphone, tablet, or sitting before a giant desktop display. This prevents frustrating horizontal scrolling and keeps text comfortable to read.
sections.code:
Welcome to Responsive Design!

Responsive pages adapt smoothly to any device.
sections.output: Displays a greeting text with a light cyan background explaining device adaptation.

sections.h: The Importance of the Viewport Meta Tag
sections.text: Before mobile-optimized screens, browsers thought they were rendering sites on huge desktop monitors and zoomed them out on tiny phones, making text microscopic and unreadable. The viewport meta tag tells the browser to use the device's actual physical width as the correct starting point.
sections.code: This text appears at a natural, ideal size on mobile thanks to the viewport tag.
sections.output: Displays readable, properly sized text thanks to the correct viewport meta tag.

sections.text: Media queries are like magical glasses for your website; they let it 'see' the screen size it is opened on. If the screen is wide, it applies one design. If it's narrow, it instantly tweaks CSS rules to fit the available space without breaking layout structure.
sections.code: Resize your browser window to see me change!
sections.output: A coral colored box turns light green when the browser window is resized smaller.

sections.text: To write a successful media query, start with `@media` followed by a condition in parentheses like `(max-width: 700px)`, then open curly braces and place inside them the CSS rules you want activated only when that screen size condition is met.
sections.code: Resize the window to change my color!
sections.output: A heading changes from dark blue to dark red when the screen gets narrow.

sections.h: Switching From Multi-Column to Single Column
sections.text: On large laptop screens, we love placing cards side-by-side to fill horizontal space. But on narrow mobile screens, these columns bunch up and become unreadable. The solution is using a media query to switch layout from multiple columns to a single vertical column spanning 100% width.
sections.code:
Card 1
Card 2
sections.output: Two cards sit side-by-side on wide screens, stacking on top of each other on narrow screens.

sections.text: Just like controlling card and text layouts, you must ensure images never break outside mobile screen bounds. By adding `max-width: 100%` and `height: auto` to images, they shrink gracefully inside narrow containers without overflowing or losing quality.
sections.code: Fluid image fitting its container:
sections.output: An image whose width adapts smoothly within its parent container.

sections.text: Smart developers start by writing base CSS styles for small screens (mobile) first, then use media queries starting with `min-width` to layer on extra styles for larger displays. This approach is faster and more performant because mobile devices don't carry extra weight they don't need.
sections.code: This text grows larger and changes background when the screen is wider than 700px.
sections.output: Text size and background color expand as the browser window becomes wider.

sections.text: You don't always need to buy a brand new phone or tablet to test your site! Modern web browsers like Firefox and Google Chrome feature built-in developer tools (Responsive Design Mode) allowing you to drag browser windows or pick device presets to preview how your site looks instantly.
sections.code: Open DevTools (F12) and try testing screen dimensions!
